# Find The Trick

A task put in front of you to measure skill is not random. Someone designed it. The signal — the part that separates a strong attempt from a weak one — almost always lives in one specific place: a constraint the obvious approach misses, an edge the textbook solution drops, a gap in the system you're working against.

Find that place first. Your code is downstream of it.

If you write code before finding it, you will write code that handles ninety percent of the task and misses the ten percent that decides the score. That is the dominant failure mode here, and no amount of polish on the other ninety percent recovers from it.

---

## The trick lives in the gap

Every problem has an obvious shape — the version a junior would recognize and start typing immediately. The obvious shape is rarely the whole problem. The score lives in the difference between the obvious shape and the real one.

To find the difference, ask:

- What would a textbook solution miss?
- What does the problem mention that a textbook problem of this kind wouldn't?
- What is the smallest extra constraint that, if added, makes the obvious approach wrong?

Three sentences, written out, before you start typing. If you can't write the third, you haven't found the trick yet — keep reading.

## Read the counterparty

Every task has a counterparty: a checker, a sanitizer, a downstream consumer, a runtime that will hit your code with input you didn't choose. If the counterparty is in the working directory, read it. If it's hinted at, find it. The trick is almost always visible there in plain text — a regex with a missing case, a comparison that uses strings where it should use values, a cleanup path that runs in one branch but not another, a date arithmetic that's inclusive on one side and exclusive on the other.

You can spend ten minutes reading the counterparty, or two hours debugging code you wrote before reading it. It's the same ten minutes either way.

## Ask what your obvious code would get wrong

Before writing your first line, write a list of three concrete inputs that would break your planned approach. Not categories — actual inputs. If you cannot name three, your model of the problem is too thin and you should keep reading until you can.

Then write the code that handles those three. The happy path will fall out for free.

## The trick is usually one of these

Skim this list before coding. Pick the categories that fit. Sometimes it is two.

- **Boundary.** Off-by-one on a range, inclusive vs exclusive, "today" as a moving anchor, the first of the month vs the last, a sliding window's edge.
- **Propagation.** A signal, an exception, a cleanup, a return value that should travel through your code but stops one frame too early.
- **Format.** A literal name, casing, separator, file shape, encoding the spec stated explicitly and the obvious abstraction quietly ignored.
- **Adversary.** An input the design plainly implies but no example shows — built to defeat the lazy filter, the lazy parser, the lazy assumption.
- **Resource.** A thing acquired but not released on every code path; a lock, a connection, a task, a subprocess.
- **Order.** Two operations whose sequence matters in a way the obvious solution does not preserve.

Most tricks fit one of these. The rest fit a combination of two. If a trick fits none of them, you've probably misidentified it.

## The "I'm done" trap

When your code passes your own runs, you have the most dangerous belief in this work: you have evidence. Evidence shifts your gut from *I should keep checking* to *I should ship*. Resist that shift.

Pass-on-your-own-runs is a low bar. The test that grades you was designed by someone who knew what was hard about this problem and built specifically for that. Before you stop, name the trick out loud, in one sentence: *"The trick was X. I handled it by doing Y."* If you can't say that sentence concretely, you have not finished — you have finished the obvious version of the task.

## When the trick won't appear

Sometimes the trick is genuinely hidden, and reading and listing don't surface it. In that case:

- Run the obvious solution and look at exactly what fails. The failure narrows the trick faster than more reading.
- Read the failure as data, not as a verdict. The diff between expected and actual is the trick made literal.
- One concrete failure beats one more theory. Get to the failure quickly, then think.

Iterating against feedback is not giving up on finding the trick — it's how you find it when reading alone won't.

---

## Before you submit — find-the-trick checklist

Run through these before declaring the task complete:

- [ ] I have named the trick in one sentence and I can point to where in the task it is hinted.
- [ ] I read the counterparty — checker, consumer, sanitizer, downstream code — if one was visible.
- [ ] I listed at least three inputs my obvious approach would fail on, before writing code.
- [ ] My final code visibly handles the trick — as code, not as a comment.
- [ ] My code's behavior on those three inputs matches what the trick demands.

If any item is missing, you have not finished. You have produced the textbook attempt.

---

## Anti-patterns

- Coding the obvious shape and trusting that the rest will work out.
- Confusing "passes my own examples" with "passes the test."
- Reading the spec but not the surrounding code that will run against your output.
- Believing a syntactically-valid solution is a correct solution.
- Wrapping the obvious approach in error handling and calling that robustness.
- Quitting after the first green run without asking what was actually checked.
- Treating the task as random — believing there is no trick, when one was put there on purpose.
